items.en: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer with Anthropic.

“I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.”

Replit sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. Under its partnership with Anthropic, Replit used the AI lab’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly.

Masad’s comments were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

There is evidence on the company’s website, blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was using Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities.
TechCrunch reached back out to Replit for clarification and will update this story if we hear back.
Masad shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue.

“We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.”
Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures.

“In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.”
This article was updated to article to include more context on Replit using Anthropic’s models.
Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
—Michal Luria, Aliya Bhatia, and Danah Boyd

Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds.
The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15.
But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented.
Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered.

I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated.

Almost 30 years later, pet owners have an expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing?
10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Form Energy and its iron batteries
As wind and solar power grow, utilities need cheaper ways to store electricity for longer periods. Form Energy aims to meet that need with batteries that can store energy for 100 hours.

The company has developed a new type of battery using iron, a far more abundant and cheaper metal than those used in many existing batteries. It uses a process that Form calls “reversible rusting,” in which iron turns to rust as the battery discharges and back to iron when it charges.

Inside the experimental world of animal infrastructure

In the mid-2000s, toads were meeting a gruesome end near Ede, a leafy old town in the Netherlands. Residents responded by building wildlife tunnels beneath the road to help them reach their breeding ponds safely.
The crossings became popular. But a few years later, researchers found the local toad population had crashed from more than 10,000 to fewer than 1,000.
The case reflects a wider global push to build wildlife crossings and other forms of “animal infrastructure.” But do they actually help animal populations recover? Read the full story to find out.

When Gerlisa Scott-Wiley found out she was pregnant, one of the first people she told was her fitness trainer. She’d been going to group fitness classes her trainer ran three times a week for the past eight years, and she wanted to make sure she could continue working out safely without harming the baby. Her trainer assured her that they’d make modifications when needed and then went further, offering to support her in a way that went beyond the gym: He wanted to be her doula.

Desmond Scott’s wife’s delivery had not been easy. She delivered their baby via C-section and was in the hospital for five days. She did not have a doula, and, looking back, Scott says there’s a lot that he wishes they’d known. “For example, she was given so much Pitocin to get things going, but I now know there are natural ways to speed things up,” Scott says. Shortly after their son was born, Scott told his wife how much he enjoyed supporting her during her pregnancy — and how much he regretted his blind spots in the delivery room — and she jokingly suggested that he become a doula, explaining to him what it was. The idea stuck with him, especially when he considered that most of his fitness clients were women in their 20s, 30s, and 40s.

The more he thought seriously about becoming a doula, the more he realized it was his chance to educate men on childbirth too. One of his friends shared that he didn’t know how to support his partner during pregnancy and post-birth. “He told me, ‘I just don’t know my role,’” Scott says. “Most men don’t have conversations with other dads about what it’s like in the delivery room. All they know is what they see in movies, like the dad passing out,” he adds. Educating men, he says, is a way to flip the script.

For Scott-Wiley (who is not related to Scott), having him as her doula was a no-brainer. “He’s someone I can trust, he’s patient with me, and his head is so full of knowledge. He’s very serious about what he’s doing,” she says.

It also helped that her husband, who trains with Scott as well, trusted him too. “My husband felt comfortable with me having a male doula because we’re showing up to the delivery room with another Black man who’s supportive of us,” she says. “Especially knowing the challenges that Black women face while giving birth in this country, it was important for us to show up feeling strong.” The fact that Scott had no idea how it felt to have contractions, give birth, or breastfeed wasn’t a deal-breaker. Her only hesitation was the intimacy of it all, letting someone who wasn’t her partner see her at her most exposed. In the end, her trust in him outweighed the potential awkwardness. If she had to do it all again, she says that she wouldn’t change a thing.

Giving birth is intimate, high stakes, and often framed as a kind of inherent wisdom, something passed down between women who have been there before. And yet, like Scott-Wiley, a small but growing number of women are opting out of the script by choosing to include a male doula, or “dude-la,” as part of their birth team.

Teddy Gant Jr., a Houston-based doula and former security guard, says that some of his clients seek him out precisely because he’s a man. Gant says he believes the women he works with feel safer in the delivery room with him there. “A lot of times, the commanding voice of a man can shift the dynamic of the room,” he says. “Some of my clients were single mothers who came to me because they didn’t have that masculine essence in the room and that’s what they wanted.”

While the birthing person is always a doula’s main priority, male doulas can also act as a translator of sorts for male partners, who often don’t know where to stand, what to do, or how to help. Instead of hovering awkwardly or panicking quietly in a corner, they’re coached into participating. Shanee White, whose male cousin served as her doula, says having him in the room gave her husband someone to turn to. “It’s hard for men to see their woman in a place of vulnerability, weak and hurting,” she says. “Even just having another man to ask questions about blood transfusions or what they think about circumcision. These are great conversations for men to have.” Scott says that this was a big motivator for him. His goal is to educate and empower male partners so much that he’s almost unnecessary by the time labor starts. By that point, he’s taught the male partners how to help their partner breathe through contractions. They know what position she wants to give birth in. They know how to safely massage her. “I’m there as backup,” he says.

For many women, the concept of a male doula isn’t just unfamiliar, it’s a hard “no.” “I personally feel that men have no business doing this work!” an anonymous commenter in a Facebook group for doulas shared. “I’d just prefer a nurturing woman’s touch,” another user shared. On Reddit, a man interested in becoming a doula asked for people’s thoughts. “Men effortlessly and expectedly take up so much space in every other area of healthcare. Why choose this space? The word ‘doula’ comes from the ancient Greek meaning ‘a woman who serves.’ I cannot imagine too many women choosing a male doula over a female doula,” one person commented. “Men do not belong in this space, period. There are some things men will never understand and that’s okay, but that’s why women are needed for this job,” commented another.

There isn’t much data on doulas — at least not the kind that breaks down sex and gender — but what does exist suggests men are still a tiny minority. According to job-search-platform Zippia, only 6 percent of doulas are men. Prinscilla Moore, the president of the international doula-certification program CAPPA, says the number of male doulas has substantially grown over the past five years. “If you look at the history of pregnancy and childbirth, men have been left out. But more men are saying that they want to be part of the journey too,” she says.
The shift, she says, has been most obvious in the Black community, where the stakes are especially high.

Black women in the U.S. are three times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes than white women. “Men are stepping up because they’re seeing what’s happening,” Moore says. “It’s not just on doctors to change things. And it’s not just on women either.”

Research consistently shows that doulas improve outcomes across the board. A 2023 review found that people with doulas were significantly less likely to experience complications or have low-birth-weight babies. A 2017 study found that women who received doula care during pregnancy were 58 percent less likely to experience postpartum depression or anxiety.

Dustin Young, a certified doula in Los Angeles, came to doula work after a devastating experience in his own family. His 21-year-old sister’s concerns during pregnancy were repeatedly dismissed by medical providers. “She felt pain and went to the doctor, but they just pushed her away, saying she was fine,” Young recalls. She delivered a stillborn baby at five months.

“The whole situation was traumatic, and I’m a solutions-based guy,” Young says. He started researching how stillbirths might be prevented and kept coming across the role doulas can play in advocacy and support. When his sister became pregnant again, he got certified.

For some men, the desire to become a doula stemmed from their own struggles during or after a partner’s birth experience. Juan Irby, an Alabama-based doula and founder of Dad to Dudla, experienced postpartum depression after his wife gave birth during the pandemic. “When my son was first born, I was like, Man, this is great. I’m a dad! But then a few weeks later, I started feeling a little funny. I felt sad. I started to Google a lot of things, including if men could get postpartum depression, and I really related to what I read. A lot of people don’t know that one in ten men experience postpartum depression,” Irby says, adding that he believes the stats are much higher due to underreporting.

He’s been working as a doula now for five years, largely focusing on the partner’s role in the birth. Irby says he teaches male partners how to do double hip squeezes, which are used during labor to relieve lower back pain and help open the pelvis, and how to swaddle a baby and change diapers, skills he says most men never learn because they likely didn’t grow up babysitting. “I tell the men, ‘Don’t think of me as your doula,’” he says. “‘Think of me as your coach. I want to give you all these tools to help you, your partner, and your baby get through this whole journey and come into this new thing we call parenthood.’”

Still, resistance to male doulas runs deep. Nikki Young, a certified doula who worked as a high-risk labor-and-delivery nurse for 17 years, believes a doula is a role that should only be filled by women. “Historically, doula work has been women helping women. There are so few female spaces these days, and I don’t want birth to lose that sacred space,” she says.

Even Moore, who supports men entering the field, acknowledges potential limitations. “Women tell their doula everything, even things they wouldn’t tell their mom or best friend,” she says. “I don’t know if a woman would be as open with a male doula.”

That question becomes especially pointed postpartum, when doulas may help with breastfeeding, an area where some clients might hesitate to take guidance from a man. Scott-Wiley says Scott gave her advice on breastfeeding prior to her giving birth, but when difficulty with nursing became a reality, he put her in touch with a female lactation expert.

For some men, the barriers aren’t theoretical; they’re structural. David Aceron, a retired Army infantryman who became a certified doula in 2010, eventually left the profession because of persistent criticism. He became interested in doula work after taking a birthing class as part of a holistic-health-practitioner program. Aceron was the only man in his certification program with DONA International, a doula-certification program, and says he wasn’t taken seriously by his peers, who questioned why he was there. “I got hit with a lot of questions, like Why do you want to be a doula? Are you perverted?” he says. After becoming certified, he struggled to gain access to birthing centers and was often excluded from professional spaces, like doula meet-ups.

“At one birthing center, the director denied me entry because she’d never heard of a male doula,” he says. She eventually relented, but only after his client — in active labor — insisted. Over time, the resistance outweighed the reward and he left the field.

For people choosing a doula, Moore says that gender is just one of the many considerations — and not always the most important one. Personality, shared values or religious beliefs, energy, and communication styles can matter just as much, if not more. “I’m a very lively, vibrant person. For someone who’s quiet, that might drive them nuts,” she says.

Aceron’s experience aside, the other male doulas say the vast majority of people have been nothing but supportive of their decision to enter the birthing field. But whether it’s praise or criticism, they say others’ opinions are just noise; what keeps them invested is the work itself.

Irby remembers one pregnancy in particular where he felt his presence made a real difference. A client had contacted him on Facebook, asking for his services because her partner was incarcerated. Throughout her pregnancy, she would text Irby questions, asking for his advice. Then one night, she messaged him at 2 a.m. It was time.

Irby showed up at the hospital 15 minutes later, meeting his client and her mother. He showed her mother how to help her breathe and rub her back. He helped his client use a peanut ball, which is an hourglass-shaped inflatable tool used to open up the pelvis, a part of her birthing plan they had talked about in advance. Around 3 a.m., his client told Irby she had to poop. “I told her, ‘Okay, that means the baby is on his way,’” Irby says.

When he called the nurses in, the baby was already making its way out through the birth canal. The labor could have been stressful, but it wasn’t. The room felt joyous and relaxed. “The nurse caught the baby and said, ‘I almost missed the moment,’” he said. Irby hadn’t.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary You Can See Everything arrives in theaters this weekend accompanied by a shroud of mystique as well as glowing reviews. My colleague Alison Willmore called YCSE “the movie of the year.” Rolling Stone’s David Fear pronounced it “simply, unabashedly, unashamedly brilliant.” The New Yorker’s Richard Brody said it’s “strangely, poetically, poignantly beautiful … a movie of dazzling conundrums and vertiginous paradoxes.”

Born out of a setup that beggars belief — weeks before heading to prison, convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes invited the filmmakers to embed with her and her family — YCSE has been handled like a priceless heirloom by its distributor, A24. For three years, the indie studio kept the doc’s very existence under wraps. This extended to its debut at the Telluride Film Festival, where the film played as a “secret screening” with no advance warning. When YCSE was added to the lineup of the New York Film Festival, there were no press screenings; the only way to see it was to finagle a ticket to the premiere, creating a frenzy that has been described to me as “feral.” For A24, this manufactured scarcity has played out exactly as planned. The film will open to a level of hype unmatched by any documentary in decades as viewers scramble to see it before its secrets get spoiled. Showings are sold out across the country, and box-office forecasts predict an opening weekend that could surpass Digger’s — an astounding feat for a three-hour documentary playing in one-fourth as many theaters.

You might think that, given these effusive reactions, You Can See Everything would thus be a natural contender for the Best Documentary Feature Oscar. But that would be overlooking one key factor: To get there, YCSE would first have to be nominated by the roughly 700 members of the Academy’s documentary branch. That’s a taller order than it sounds, because the doc branch is not like other branches. No other branch takes such delight in going its own way, regularly giving a cold shoulder to titles the rest of the industry adores. No other branch’s members prioritize their role as combatants in an ideological battle — in this case, over what a documentary should be. This is the branch I’m most familiar with — many of its members are documentary professionals based in New York — and yet I feel I don’t understand it at all.

That reputation stems from the sense that the doc branch can be insular, cliquish, and vicious. “They’re a hard group of people to please,” Meerza said. Their forebears at the Academy snubbed canonical documentaries like The Thin Blue Line, Roger & Me, and Hoop Dreams. (The Hoop Dreams snub is credited with inspiring the creation of the doc branch; before, nominations were determined by a self-selected committee of Oscars voters, which tended to be older and more conservative.) With so many documentaries to choose from — last season over 200 titles were eligible — and, crucially, so many different types of documentaries, the branch tends to default to a predictable vision of what an Oscar-nominated documentary should look like. This vision tends not to look like the kind of docs preferred by the wider Academy (who will be voting on the winner), and it also tends not to look very much like You Can See Everything.

A core tenet of the branch’s philosophy is that a documentary should tackle weighty subjects. Back in 2009, Entertainment Weekly’s Owen Gleiberman slammed the doc branch for ignoring “movies that were seen, praised, and loved” in favor of projects “about well-meaning social and political themes.” (Last season’s nominees included films about Russian propaganda, gun violence, cancer, and abuses within the prison system.) Stylistically, it tends to prefer unobtrusive, down-the-middle filmmaking, rather than docs that are highly stylized or in which the filmmaker is front and center. “For most people in the doc branch, their distinction of what a documentary is falls more under the guise of journalism,” Meerza said. “There seems to be real resistance to anything that could be classed as entertainment.”

The second is that it tends not to nominate films about famous people, particularly when they’re made in collaboration with the subject. This may be an understandable reaction when you consider how much people outside the doc branch simply love to vote for any documentary involving a Hollywood celebrity. American Symphony, Will & Harper, My Mom Jayne — all were showered with trophies by precursor awards ceremonies and, not coincidentally, all were DOA with voters in the doc branch.

The third is that it increasingly prefers international documentaries. The doc branch has grown rapidly as the Academy has gotten more global, and today almost a third of its members come from outside the U.S. As a result, there are usually at least two international docs nominated each year; in the 2023 lineup, all five nominees were from outside the United States. An American film hasn’t won the trophy since Summer of Soul in 2022. (This point Meerza doesn’t have a problem with: “American people are not funding the best documentaries, generally speaking, these days.”)

By many accounts, the doc branch’s preferences hardened into dogma after what happened in the 2021 season. That year’s nominees included critically acclaimed docs like Crip Camp and Time — only for the broader Academy to hand the Oscar to My Octopus Teacher, the heartwarming tale of a man falling in love with a mollusk. The branch was irate. “I’ve never seen a reaction to a win like that before,” Meerza said. “People were posting pictures on social media of restaurant meals of octopus with knives stuck in them.” Since then, the scuttlebutt goes, members of the doc branch have determined that their fellow Academy voters cannot be trusted with lighter fare. They will be served only vegetables, and they will like it.

There’s one further wrinkle. Remember, only Academy members who have seen all the nominees in a given category are allowed to cast a vote on the final ballot. By excluding films that might appeal to the median Oscar voter, the functional effect is that, as a producer once put it to me, “the doc branch picks the winner.”

All of this would seem to be bad news for You Can See Everything, an American doc about a convicted scammer, starring a guy who once posed shirtless on the cover of New York Magazine, that piles up so many metafictional twists some viewers question whether it should be considered a documentary at all.

Then there’s the personal side to consider. Part of the doc branch’s reputation for pettiness comes from its willingness to snub filmmakers for extratextual reasons: If they’ve won too recently, if they’ve got the wrong distributor, or if the branch plain doesn’t like them. “Nathan is a comedian and Lance is 30 years old,” Meerza said. “There is a lot of founded or unfounded jealousy about the fact that someone that young, or someone who is not strictly speaking a documentarian, is getting to make a film with these kinds of resources behind it.” Throw in the branch’s penchant for pulling the rug out from under the title outsiders assume is the front-runner — they’ll be the ones to decide that, thank you very much — and many Oscars-watchers assume that YCSE will likely be left out of the Documentary Feature lineup on nomination morning. (I should note that there are plenty of worthy docs more likely to make the cut, including Once Upon a Time in Harlem and NAZA.)

Before seeing the film, I was skeptical. Could a movie that might be A24’s third-biggest awards priority really do something no other doc has ever done? But after catching the NYFF premiere — where, admittedly, it benefitted from an extremely friendly audience, since everyone in the room felt as if they were one of the lucky ones — I’m ready to drink the Kool-Aid. Few other films this year have made me feel the way YCSE did: marveling at where it might go next, fully satisfied at where it ended up, unable to stop turning it over in my mind. Academy voters do not seem to be immune from the hype. Per Meerza, even members of the doc branch are rushing to get tickets.

No matter whether the doc branch gets onboard, Meerza sees only good things coming for the nonfiction industry out of the whole YCSE experience: “Fundamentally, its financial success should help a lot of the people who stopped investing in feature documentaries to be like, Oh, I can still make money here.” And if the fever dream of a Best Picture nomination does come true, well, YCSE’s haters just might become its waiters at the table of success.

“As petty at the doc branch could potentially be about this film, I think if it got nominated for Best Picture, people would rally around it,” Meerza said. “If it gets nominated for Best Picture, every doc-branch member would vote for it.”

Every week between now and January 21, when the nominations for the Academy Awards are announced, Vulture will consult its crystal ball to determine the changing fortunes in this year’s Oscar race. In our “Oscar Futures” column, we’ll let you in on insider gossip, parse brand-new developments, and track industry buzz to figure out who’s up, who’s down, and who’s currently leading the race for a coveted Oscar nomination.

The queer Spanish Civil War epic hits theaters this weekend on the back of months of stellar press. First out of Cannes, where Bola Negra livened up a sleepy year on the Croisette before being snapped up by Netflix. (The streamer is giving it a 47-day theatrical window, its longest runway yet.) Then at TIFF, the film proved its populist bona fides by taking home the People’s Choice Award, an Oscar bellwether that suggests audiences are keying into La Bola Negra’s grand melodrama. If there is an Odyssey alternative lurking somewhere out there, could this heart-forward contender be it?

Up ⬆ Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, La Bola Negra

After tying Paweł Pawlikowski for Cannes’ Best Director prize, the men known as Los Javis should make for strong competition in this race. Not only should La Bola Negra’s historic sweep and tripartite structure impress this auteur-friendly branch, their distinct directorial sensibility (“What if the Spanish Civil War looked like a spread from A&F Quarterly?”) could resonate with voters seeking an alternative to the usual art-house understatement. It doesn’t hurt either that, as a former “It” couple who broke up during production, they’ll bring an irresistible personal narrative to the trail.

With Los Javis looking all but assured of a nom, the requisite international directing spot appears to be accounted for — but why stop at just one? Neon is pushing All of a Sudden’s Ryusuke Hamaguchi and Fjord’s Cristian Mungiu, but I wonder if Lee could represent a compelling alternative. The Korean auteur was the subject of a meaty New Yorker profile this week that detailed his political convictions and novelistic eye, qualities that are on ample display in his first film since Burning. One caveat: Like La Bola Negra, Possible Love is a Netflix film, putting it in danger of becoming the Jan Brady of the streamer’s awards slate.

Just this week, luminaries like Neil Young and Hideo Kojima came out of the woodwork to proclaim the film a misunderstood masterpiece. Clearly not everyone is ready to shovel dirt into the grave of this campaign, so Cruise remains in the race for now, even if everything I wrote two weeks ago remains true.

We're now 40 years on from the worst nuclear disaster in history, and scientists have been analyzing radioactive particles blown out by Chornobyl to see what's left of the fuel that got scattered – and what state those particles are in.

Knowing how these chemical pellets have held up to decades of weathering and decay is valuable for understanding the safety of nuclear plants in the future – and for working out when it might be safe to return to the Chornobyl site without a protective suit.
What stood out most from the analysis was the "remarkably persistent" structure of the radioactive dust particles, which showed much more stability than expected.
That means most of the radioactive material remains locked inside.
The researchers behind the work, from Leibniz University Hannover and the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR) in Germany, have published their findings in the Journal of Hazardous Materials.

Six fuel particles were analyzed in total, split into three categories depending on what happened to them during the original reactor explosion. Some, for example, had melted and bonded with their coating of zirconium.
"There are three classes of these particles," says physicist Tobias Weissenborn, from Leibniz University Hannover.
"First, there are particles that are chemically and physically still very similar to the nuclear fuel uranium dioxide.
"Then, there are particles that are partially or fully encased in, or completely fused with, their zirconium layer. The third type of particle was created when the graphite moderator caught fire."

Each of these particle classes has ended up with a different chemical composition, which can affect how they degrade. The sampled particles measured a mere 8–50 micrometers in size (so at least 20 would fit inside a single millimeter), and were all collected from inside the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone.
A technique known as diffraction analysis was used to look inside these microscopic specks, with the atomic crystal structure being determined through the way X-rays reflected away from it.
"Ultimately, we fully rotated the particles in an X-ray beam focused down to 100 micrometers – about the thickness of a human hair," says crystallographer Christoph Hennig from HZDR.
"We measured each particle from 2,000 different angles to seamlessly capture all the reflections."

Across all three particle types, the researchers found the structure holding the nuclear fuel had largely remained intact. That suggests a greater chemical stability in these fuel specks than previously assumed.

The study also gives scientists a better idea of how these particle groups are put together – exactly how the disaster and its subsequent chemical chain reaction shifted the composition of the fuel crystals.
"Our findings demonstrate that Chornobyl fuel particles act as remarkably persistent reservoirs," write the researchers in their published paper.
The researchers frame this as potentially good news: It means the particles may be releasing radioactive material into the environment more slowly than previously assumed.
While it's not safe to go back, the findings could help scientists better assess the long-term environmental risks.

The radioactive material hasn't gone anywhere, which means these particles will remain dangerous for decades. Breathing these particles in is still going to be extremely hazardous to health, and they could get kicked up from the ground by wind, erosion, or passing animals.

The researchers also acknowledge that six particles – all sourced from two locations – are a small sample. Weighing up the current risks in Chornobyl will require more comprehensive sets of data collected over longer periods.
"Even if we obtained some averages at some point, we still wouldn't be able to make universal statements about health risks in the region," says Weissenborn.
"Even if the particles decay in a largely uniform pattern, there will always be outliers, more persistent particles, that will release radionuclides at a later point in time."
The research has been published in Journal of Hazardous Materials.

A Golden Dome task force established under U.S. Northern Command earlier this year has a broad remit, which includes fielding the capability to defend the U.S. against missile and drone attacks, its leaders said this week. Some of the primary focuses right now are ensuring Golden Dome can defend itself against cyber threats and that it will work in the real world.

NORTHCOM established the group, dubbed Joint Task Force-Gold, in January. It is led by the head of the Army’s Space and Missile Defense Command, Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, with Army Col. Kevin Stonerook as his deputy.

Speaking with reporters Oct. 14 at the annual Association of the U.S. Army conference in Washington D.C., Stonerook said the task force has about 100 personnel based at Peterson Space Force Base, Colo. The team works closely with SMDC to integrate and coordinate Golden Dome capabilities across the air and missile defense enterprise.

Practically, that includes a range of responsibilities, including leading site surveys for future Golden Dome locations—the first confirmed hub is in Fort Story, Va.—and providing expert operators to inform the architecture. Stonerook said that lately one of the group’s major focuses has been on building a team to develop a defensive cyber capability for Golden Dome, or GDA.

“We are helping put together the team of teams, all the different stakeholders—be that vendors and other government agencies—to really provide a cyber warfare capability for GDA,” he said. “That’s one of the main things that we’re really focused on.”

The Pentagon envisions Golden Dome as a sweeping network of sensors, satellites, and interceptors designed to protect the United States from an array of air and missile threats—from drones to ballistic missiles to hypersonic weapons. The architecture will depend on a command-and-control network to connect and orchestrate its many parts. Golden Dome Director Gen. Michael Guetlein has described the C2 system as the program’s “glue layer.”

The Army’s Space and Missile Defense Command plays a key role in the Golden Dome plan. The command already has an important role in operating the limited anti-missile defense for the U.S. homeland that was first fielded more than 20 years ago. It is responsible for approximately 40 Ground-Based Midcourse Defense interceptors that protect America from ballistic missile attacks as well as the National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System surrounding Washington.

“We have the most experienced air defense force we’ve ever had,” Rafferty said in an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “It’s a mission that we do already with the ground-based interceptors in Alaska and under SMDC, and in the defense of the National Capital Region and other key locations in the homeland. We’re going to scale that. We have people who do that 24/7, 365, and have, for many years: an incredible base to build on.”

The Army is also responsible for missile defense across the globe. Iran’s attacks on U.S. forces in the Middle East have taxed and tested the Army’s THAAD and Patriot ballistic missile defense batteries. The U.S. has sent Army air defenders and air defense systems from Europe and Asia to the Middle East and has expended hundreds of Patriot and THAAD interceptors to combat Iranian ballistic missiles, which have become increasingly more advanced. The Army, in turn, has tried to learn from the flurry of attacks.

Golden Dome will use some existing technology, but its overall goal of creating a comprehensive missile defense shield will require cutting-edge and novel tech too. Joint Task Force-Gold is seeking to bring real-world experience into the picture.
“They’re in a sprint to deliver materiel,” Rafferty said. “We better be ready to train it, to man it, to have the right organization, the sustainment for it.”

Rafferty compared bringing those issues to ones he faced earlier in his career leading the Army’s Long Range Precision Fires Cross-Functional Team, the Army’s effort to modernize surface-to-surface weapons. He wanted to deliver equipment “as quickly as we could.” But personnel needed to learn how to use it. “The rest of everybody was sprinting to, ‘Hey, how are we going to fight with this thing?’”

Likewise, JTF-Gold is to attempt to ease the transition of Golden Dome from concept to reality. By working with the Pentagon’s Golden Dome office—officially titled the Direct Reporting Program Manager—to develop capability, Rafferty says JTF-Gold’s goal is to examine how the system will work on a practical basis.

In support of the Pentagon’s push to field an initial Golden Dome capability by 2028, JTF-Gold has also hosted a series of planning sprints, bringing together all of the companies and agencies working on the program “to really focus on operationalizing GDA,” Stonerook said. The task force held the first of these events in February in Colorado Springs, Colo., and drew more than 300 people. The next one is scheduled for late October.

The task force has also been involved in the large-scale test events run by the Golden Dome program office. Over the past year, the program has conducted at least two tests, which officials say were successful, though they haven’t discussed the objectives or outcome in detail.
Rafferty said the tests helped JTF-Gold better understand what it might take to one day operate the capability.

“Some of the testing events that the DPRM’s office has run have been really instructive about the types of soldiers that we need to man this,” Rafferty said. JTF-Gold is “bringing those issues to light and then creating opportunities for learning about the systems as they’re coming out, so the teams can lean forward on what the training package is or what kind of individuals we need.”
“We have the most experienced, combat-proven air defense force in the world ready to come and help man an expanded Gordon Dome from America,” Rafferty said.

Blue Origin said it will add new launch pads on Florida’s Space Coast to help ramp up the flight rate of its New Glenn rockets, as the company recovers from a catastrophic test fire explosion in May.

In a series of other infrastructure announcements Friday morning, Ian Richardson, the Senior Vice President of Operations at Blue Origin, said the company was serious about launching and landing more rockets.

“These investments are centered on one goal: building the capacity to support more missions, more reliably, and more efficiently,” Richardson said. “As we look ahead, this infrastructure is designed to support multiple flights per week by the end of the decade.”

The new pads would be modeled after Blue Origin facilities at Launch Complex 36 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. LC-36A, which is being rebuilt after the static test fire explosion, serves the New Glenn 7×2 rocket and LC-36B is under construction to support launches of the 9×4 variant of the rocket, which features nine BE-4 engines on the first stage and four BE-3U engines on the upper stage. The announcement did not reveal the exact locations of the new pad facilities.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is in the middle of a 30-day comment period as it seeks public input on Blue Origin’s request to increase its launch cadence at LC-36A from 12 permitted flights up to 50. A virtual public hearing is scheduled for Thursday, Oct. 22, and public comment closes on Oct. 30.

With more pads coming online, Blue Origin said it will also introduce two new landing vessels to its marine fleet. Returned boosters will be serviced at the company’s new vertical integration facility, which is currently under construction just down the road from LC-36.
Simultaneously, a payload processing facility that can be used by both Blue Origin and others is being built in partnership with the U.S. Space Force.

On the manufacturing side, Blue Origin is investing $330 million in an expansion at their Rocket Park site to support the production of upper stages for the New Glenn 9×4 rockets. The 1.37-million-square-foot facility is anticipated to be completed by the summer of 2027 and would support the creation of up to 150 upper stages annually.

“Blue Origin has invested more than $3 billion in facilities and infrastructure across the state. More than 5,000 employees and 500 Florida suppliers support our work today,” Richardson said. “Our manufacturing and operations footprint has more than doubled in the last couple of years, now spanning more than 20 sites across Brevard and Orange Counties.”

Richardson said they have also made investments into the production of payload fairings, which are made in-house. In early May, Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp mentioned on social media that the company was working towards a plan to recover and refurbish its fairings for reuse.

“Our investments also build the capability to bring in raw materials and manufacture nearly all of our components, systems, and products in-house,” Richardson said. “Paired with our network of external supplier partners, this creates a resilient, responsive pipeline designed to keep our factories supplied as we increase our production rate.”
Blue Origin’s founder Jeff Bezos said in an interview with Fox News earlier this month that the company is still pushing to fly its New Glenn 7×2 rocket again before the end of the year.

This New Glenn push comes as Blue Origin is also in the very early stages of bringing New Glenn launch capabilities to the West Coast. Back in April, the U.S. Space Force selected Blue Origin to pursue final discussions on developing Space Launch Complex 14 at the southern end of Vandenberg Space Force Base.
SLC-14 is an undeveloped launch site and would need to go through a full environmental review before significant development moves forward.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has named Stephen Cash director of the agency’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, effective Monday, Oct. 19. Cash, a veteran NASA engineer and aerospace executive, returns to lead the center where he began his career more than four decades ago.

“Marshall contributions to NASA’s missions are historic and it’s no question why it’s the Center of Excellence for propulsion,” said Isaacman. “Steve Cash is a Marshall legend, has spent his career around the hardware, the people and has been in the seat before making the decisions when human spaceflight is on the line. As Marshall continues its critical role in Artemis and takes on new challenges in advanced propulsion, nuclear power, and the systems that will carry us deeper into the solar system, Steve brings the experience, technical judgment, and mission focus needed to lead the center into that next chapter. I am also grateful to Rae Ann Meyer for the leadership she has provided to Marshall during this transition and for her continued service to NASA.”

“Leading a NASA center requires a commitment to its people and to the technical capabilities entrusted to them,” said Amit Kshatriya, NASA associate administrator and chief engineer. “Steve understands that the jewel of Marshall is its workforce and that engineering excellence is sustained by giving talented people the opportunity to design, build, test, and learn through hands-on work. As Marshall continues strengthening the manufacturing, structural loads and dynamics, and propulsion capabilities that underpin NASA’s exploration enterprise, Steve’s leadership will help ensure the workforce has opportunities to develop and apply the expertise needed to deliver the agency’s most ambitious missions.”

As center director, Cash will lead one of NASA’s largest field centers, overseeing a workforce of more than 5,000 civil service and contractor employees and a broad portfolio of propulsion, space systems, scientific research, and technology development activities. Marshall plays a critical role in NASA’s Artemis program, including the development of NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket, management of the Human Landing System Program, as well as other capabilities supporting sustained exploration of the Moon and future missions to Mars. Further, Marshall plays a key role in the advancement of nuclear power and propulsion, an area of focus that is expected to grow as NASA works towards sending the first humans to Mars.

“It is a profound honor to be back home at the Marshall Space Flight Center,” said Cash. “I am humbled to stand alongside the brilliant minds here as we continue to turn the impossible into everyday history.”

Cash began his NASA career at Marshall in 1982 and spent 34 years with the agency, holding senior engineering and management positions supporting some of the nation’s most significant human spaceflight programs.

During his NASA career, Cash served as manager of Marshall’s Space Shuttle Propulsion Office, overseeing critical propulsion systems supporting shuttle through its final missions. He later served as director of Marshall’s Safety and Mission Assurance Directorate from 2011 until his retirement in 2016, providing leadership in safety, reliability, and quality engineering to support mission success across the center.

Following his retirement from NASA, Cash continued his work in the aerospace industry, including serving as vice president for advanced space systems at Axient, supporting the development and execution of major spaceflight programs. In 2024, he was inducted into the Alabama Engineering Hall of Fame in recognition of his contributions to engineering and the nation’s space program.

Cash succeeds Rae Ann Meyer, who has served as Marshall’s acting center director since September 2025. Meyer, who previously served as Marshall’s deputy center director and associate director, has provided leadership and continuity across the center’s programs and operations during her tenure as acting director. Meyer will return to her role as Deputy Center Director.

Established in 1960, Marshall has played a central role in American space exploration for more than six decades, from developing the Saturn rockets that carried astronauts to the Moon during Apollo to advancing the propulsion systems, infrastructure, and technologies supporting the next era of human spaceflight.
