What does it mean to be a man? In the early 21st century, masculinity is contested and fraught with anxiety; influencers offer models of manliness involving fast cars, sexual conquests, and building up muscle. Before the rise of feminism, they suggest, in some supposed Golden Age, everyone had a shared sense of what it meant to be a man – and being a man was unproblematically good. The Roman Empire, in their view, offers men today an inspirational example of power, hierarchy and achievement, which is why men think about it so much – unlike women, who are too immersed in their feelings…

Manliness certainly was celebrated in the works of Cicero, republican Rome’s most eloquent statesman. In the mid-1st century BCE, his persuasive powers in the law courts and the senate were second to none; his speeches went on to inspire would-be orators well into the 20th century. He is often seen as the very embodiment of the Roman republic. The political world in which he flourished was a self-consciously masculine one; to be accused of acting like a woman was, for a Roman man, a grievous insult. Yet in Cicero’s writing we can find other strains too.

For Roman men, anything labelled feminine was necessarily to be avoided, something to be ashamed of. But what exactly did it mean to act like a man? Ancient Rome in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE saw the rise of a succession of military leaders who were promoted as masculine role models. The great general Marius won a series of victories in Spain, North Africa and on Italy’s northern frontier. For several years in a row, he was elected consul, one of Rome’s two chief executive officers. Unlike many other Roman politicians, he didn’t have an aristocratic background. One Roman writer imagines Marius fending off accusations that he was coarse in his manners:
elegance is becoming to women but toil to men. All virtuous men ought to have more fame than riches. Arms, not fine trappings, bring glory.
– from The War Against Jugurtha by Sallust
(All translations are adapted from the Loeb Classical Library.)
Here was a model of manliness forged on the battlefield.

Given the military might of ancient Rome, it is surely unsurprising that Romans often associated masculinity with courage in battle. The word virtus, a term cognate with the Roman vir (meaning man as opposed to woman), clearly means ‘courage in war’ when it is first recorded in the mid-5th century BCE. Courage in battle could be taken as the foremost manifestation of Roman masculinity. The historian Sallust, writing in the 40s BCE, praises earlier generations of Romans for their pre-eminent manliness in war: ‘whenever their virtus repelled dangers, they rendered aid to their allies and friends.’ And yet, while Rome continued to boast ever more notable military successes in the middle and later republic (from the 3rd to the 1st century BCE), the battlefield was by no means the only arena in which Roman masculinity might be put to the test.

When Cicero was 16, like others of his social standing, his transition to adulthood was marked by a special ceremony, most likely at the feast of the Liberalia in 90 BCE. This was the moment when he first put on the toga of manhood, a cumbersome length of woollen fabric worn by Roman citizen men, a garment associated with civilian as opposed to military life. Years later, as consul in 63 BCE, Cicero played a leading role in uncovering and suppressing a conspiracy against the Roman state, and boasted that this was a victory won by ‘citizens in togas’. It was his speeches that had convinced his fellow senators and the Roman people of the dangers posed by Catiline’s conspiracy, leading to decisive action against those involved. Cicero had used his voice as consul to save Rome, he declared in a speech a few years later. Throughout his life, he insisted his victory was comparable to those of Rome’s greatest generals. Masculine achievements weren’t confined to the battlefield; rhetoric and oratory could also conquer.

By the time he secured the consulship, Cicero was regarded as Rome’s top orator. Public speaking was highly prized by members of Rome’s governing elite. Its end result mattered hugely – winning over one’s listeners. But the way Rome’s politicians spoke and even how they dressed could also serve to demonstrate their manliness. Codes of civilian masculinity governed behaviour in public spaces such as the Forum, the law-courts and the senate. Markers of manliness in this sphere were subject to relentless public scrutiny. As the later expert on oratory Quintilian put it, the orator’s dress needs to be ‘resplendent and manly: for when it comes to one’s toga and shoes and hair, excessive care as well as negligence are equally blameable’. The toga, for instance, must be correctly draped; he notes a little later, ‘throwing back the fold from its bottom onto the right shoulder is foppish and effeminate’.

Orators were alert to the niceties of their own – and one another’s – masculine self-fashioning. In the cacophonous world of the Roman republic, politicians, advocates and those aspiring to a public role exchanged no-holds-barred insults. Often, they cast aspersions on one another’s masculinity, with disparaging comments on an opponent’s way of speaking, his gestures, the way he wore his toga – as well as his sexual behaviour. Orators would be praised for speaking in a ‘manly’ way. And they were robustly attacked for any ‘effeminate’ deviations in their style and manner of speech. Some orators favoured a more elaborate style fashionable in the long-established rhetorical schools of the eastern Mediterranean, the zone the Romans called Asia. Contrasts were drawn between ‘Asian’ style and the plainer style associated with Athenian rhetorical tradition. The Asian style was regularly denigrated as ‘effeminate’. Yet too ‘unpolished’ a style could seem old-fashioned, even coarse. Moderation was itself celebrated as a quintessentially masculine quality. But where to draw the line?
Quintilian criticised rhetoric teachers who encourage their students to show off

In the late republic, attempts were made to codify guidance to aspiring orators. An anonymous treatise on rhetoric addressed To Herennius promises to help its reader present himself as a proper man through training in public speech. The author advises, for instance, against any sharp exclamation that ‘injures the voice and likewise jars the hearer, for it has about it something ignoble, suited rather to feminine outcry than to manly dignity in speaking.’ In On the Orator, Cicero has a character emphasise the importance of appropriate gestures in seeking to arouse particular emotions in one’s listeners: ‘all these emotions must be accompanied by gesture – … with this vigorous manly throwing out of the chest, borrowed not from the stage and the theatrical profession but from the parade ground or even from wrestling.’ The theatre had morally dubious associations; actors were often branded effeminate. Performer though he was, an orator would do well to cultivate a more military aura and disguise the degree to which his art drew on dramatic technique.

Writing a century after Cicero, Quintilian was a huge admirer of his work, regarding him as the ideal model for the aspiring public speaker. In Quintilian’s wide-ranging treatise on the education of the ideal orator, sound ethical character but also manliness are presented as essential qualifications: ‘I am training the consummate orator, a figure whose existence is predicated on his being a good man [vir bonus].’ Quintilian expresses his disapproval of speeches composed merely for display, a widespread practice in his day, criticising teachers of rhetoric who encourage their students to show off:

The teachers, I feel bound to say, have been guilty of the same offence as slave dealers who castrate boys to increase their attractions. As those dealers think there is no beauty in strength or in a muscular arm, and certainly not in a beard and the other natural endowments of the male, and so take what might, if left alone, have developed into sturdiness and soften its supposed hardness – so do we cover up the manly form of eloquence and the power of lean and vigorous speech with a delicate veneer of style, and think effectiveness of no importance, so long as everything is smooth and polished.

This simile – shocking in multiple ways to a modern reader – aligns the recommended mode of speech with the embodiment characteristic of the free, adult, bodily intact male. Indeed, the right kind of speech makes clear the laudable moral character and manliness of the speaker: ‘I decline to regard as eloquence in any sense something which shows no trace at all of a normal male, let alone of a man of weight and integrity,’ Quintilian continues.

But there was of course a paradox in all this effort focused on generating an impression of authentic masculinity, a paradox apparent in the advice in To Herennius to ‘make everything seem straight from the heart’. The artifice required to generate authentic-seeming masculinity was all too evident. We can see this as a symptom of the ongoing challenge of justifying male supremacy, through assertions of the ‘natural’ superiority of men to women (and indeed of free men to enslaved ones). What exactly was ‘masculine’ rhetorical style? Opinions could differ significantly. But masculinity itself was always a positive term. And giving effective speeches in Rome’s public spaces was an ideal way to communicate one’s specifically masculine virtue.

What happened, though, when a member of Rome’s elite, once renowned for his eloquence, found himself cut off from the Forum and the senate? Cicero’s role in the punishment of those who had conspired with Catiline was controversial; Roman citizens had been executed without trial – a breach of the rights of the Roman people. In 58 BCE, following the manoeuvrings of his political enemy Clodius, Cicero was unceremoniously exiled. He languished far from Rome for 16 months, often fearing for his life, separated from family and friends – but also from access to the public arena where he’d held his own for so long. His letters home are full of lamentation. To his old friend Atticus, Cicero communicates his utter misery and despair. He often wishes he were dead. Reflecting on his losses felt like tearing open a wound: ‘I mourn the loss not only of the things and persons that were mine but of my very self. What am I now?’

Cicero was criticised by his contemporaries (and by later commentators) for his emotional reaction to exile. Should he have adopted a Stoic stiff upper lip, perhaps? To have been unaffected by this experience would have been inhuman rather than manly, he asserts in a speech given after his return in 57 BCE:

I could not now describe my action as praiseworthy or say that I was the source of any benefit to the republic, if I had but abandoned, for the republic’s sake, what I felt no pang at losing; I should hold that such mental apathy, like the physical apathy which does not feel the sting of fire, was brute insensibility rather than bravery [virtus].
In his own way, he claimed, even his retreat into exile, and even his frequent complaints, had shown bravery – manliness.
Cicero, eloquent exponent of Roman republican values, struggled to articulate his political disappointment

Back in Rome, however, Cicero remained anxious. Generals in command of large armies – Julius Caesar, above all – asserted their dominance over the state. Rome’s senate felt increasingly powerless. ‘The republic is an empty husk,’ Cicero lamented in a letter to Atticus in 54 BCE. Another celebrated general, Pompey, eventually led the challenge to bring Caesar under control. Yet, even if this was an attempt to shore up traditional modes of government where the senate exercised greatest authority, it ended in failure – and there were also doubts about Pompey’s intentions. Was he too, perhaps, aiming at one-man rule? Following a bitter civil war lasting from 49 to 45 BCE, a victorious Julius Caesar ruled the Roman world as dictator. Cicero, Rome’s foremost orator and long at the centre of its political life, was in despair. Throughout his career, he had championed a traditional political order in which Rome’s elite competed against one another in elections and took collective decisions in the senate. This was above all a culture of robust debate, in which persuasive speech played a critical role. But now the Forum was silent. In the senate, no one dared speak against Caesar.

Cicero, most eloquent exponent of Roman republican values, struggled to articulate his profound political disappointment. This was an experience compounded by devastating personal bereavement. In 45 BCE, shortly after giving birth to a little boy, Cicero’s daughter Tullia died. He was knocked sideways. Friends wrote letters of consolation. A long letter from one, Servius Sulpicius Rufus, observed that at least Tullia, dying when she did, avoided witnessing the end of the republic. In an equally lengthy reply, Cicero acknowledged his friend’s kindness – but disputed the claim that any comfort might be found in the timing of Tullia’s death. He contrasted his own situation with that of earlier Roman public figures, who had managed to avoid giving in to personal griefs by devoting themselves to public service: ‘the high standing they derived from public life soothed their mourning’. In current political circumstances, Cicero no longer had a part in public life. He couldn’t bear even the sight of the senate – the scene of his former triumphs. In these wretched political times, it was Tullia who had been Cicero’s one source of comfort. She was ‘a haven of refuge and repose, one in whose conversation and sweet ways I put aside all cares and sorrows.’ And now she was gone.

The collapse of the Roman state in its traditional form was something Cicero had been lamenting, at least on and off, for some years. He often used the language of death, bereavement and mourning in relation to the political situation. ‘For a long time it has been my part to mourn our liberties,’ he wrote to his old friend Atticus. Just a short while before Tullia’s death, he wrote to another friend: ‘I have already grieved for the state more deeply and longer than any mother for her only child.’ It is impossible to disentangle Cicero’s devastation at the loss of his daughter from his feelings of loss at the drastic transformation of Rome’s political landscape. The one loss intensified his grief at the other. And as Cicero’s words comparing himself to a bereaved mother suggest, he experienced both the loss and the intense grief it provoked as profoundly emasculating. He could no longer be the man he once was.

And yet perhaps another sphere of activity might offer scope for a new kind of self-actualisation, a new way for a man of Cicero’s extraordinary talents to win fame through service to the state and his fellow Romans. Even before Tullia’s death, Cicero had been increasingly immersing himself in philosophy. In 46 BCE, he had written to Sulpicius of his retreat from public-speaking: ‘seeing there is no further place in the Senate House or Forum for the craft which I have studied, I have devoted all my time and attention to philosophy.’ In changed political circumstances, with the dictator Caesar as Rome’s sole ruler, philosophy felt like a kind of salvation.

Cicero’s focus in his writings of these years was on a range of mainly ethical issues, particularly the nature of virtus – now taken in a sense much closer to the English term ‘virtue’ or ‘moral excellence’. A particular concern was the management of emotions in the pursuit of spiritual wellbeing. This was an issue of pressing personal significance to Cicero following his family bereavement but also of broader relevance to those who mourned the political changes in Rome.
It is about what it means to be a man and how manhood can be forged in – and by – challenging circumstances

Cicero (and other Roman writers), influenced by Greek philosophical explorations of virtue, might sometimes attribute to women virtue of a more generalised kind. But the Latin term virtus never completely lost its association with masculinity. Noting the word’s derivation, Cicero observes in his treatise on the management of emotions, the Tusculan Disputations:
the proper virtue of a man is above all courage, whose particular functions are contempt for death and pain. We must exercise these qualities if we wish to be virtuous, indeed if we wish to be men.

Closely concerned with philosophical approaches to dealing with grief and the fear of death, this treatise is also about what it means to be a man and how manhood can be forged in – and by – challenging circumstances. ‘For surely virtue [virtus] gives sufficient to make us live bravely; if bravely, sufficient too to make us high-souled and in fact never appalled by any event and always undefeated,’ he asserts. Similar concerns surface in other works he wrote around this time: in On Ends, he stresses the importance of self-control – which he defines as avoiding behaviour that’s ‘unmanly’ – parum virile.

Cicero’s philosophical writings were themselves an act of public service, he insisted. Through setting out philosophical ideas in Latin, he was offering a way for his fellow citizens to encounter the highest kind of learning. It was a particular comfort for Cicero in a time of deep political crisis, he declared, that this moment might see the birth of philosophy in Latin.

Cicero did return, albeit briefly, to the public arena in the last year of his life. Following Caesar’s assassination, his erstwhile deputy Mark Antony manoeuvred to take over Caesar’s following and resources. Cicero thought he too was aiming at dictatorship, and gave a series of speeches, attempting to rally his fellow senators behind the ‘liberators’ and against Antony. These speeches, known as the Philippics, were a dazzling return to form.

In the second Philippic, Cicero insisted at length and in colourful detail on the ways in which Antony was a slave to bodily pleasures – a man with no capacity for self-control. Cicero dredged up a story from years previously alleging Antony had had a homosexual affair with another Roman elite man, Curio, a relationship in which Antony willingly played a ‘passive’ role: ‘No slave boy bought to satisfy lust was ever so completely in his master’s power as you were in Curio’s,’ he fulminated. The lust here is implicitly Curio’s, not Antony’s – but this willingness to subordinate himself revealed Antony’s ‘slavish’ disposition. Such sexual ‘passivity’ in an elite male – taking what was seen as a ‘feminine’, receptive sexual role – was deeply shocking for Romans. It is notable that in his swansong Cicero does his utmost to paint Antony as a man of ‘unmanly’ sexual habits, addicted to pleasure and with no sense of masculine moderation. Cicero, ever the rhetorician out to win the argument, was quite prepared to exploit his audience’s masculinist prejudices to demean an enemy.

With these speeches, Cicero managed to rally his fellow senators, at least for a time, but, in the end, the power of those who commanded the legions was unstoppable. In 43 BCE, Antony eventually joined forces with Julius Caesar’s great-nephew and heir, Octavian. They rapidly gained control of the Roman Empire – and engineered the deaths of prominent opponents, among them Cicero. When a posse of legionaries finally caught up with him, Cicero is said to have offered them his neck, meeting his end with great bravery.

Military might prevailed for the time being, underpinning the regime of Rome’s emperors which was established a few years after Cicero’s death. Yet long after the Roman empire had fallen, his writings and reflections on the nature of educated masculinity would continue to influence European elites. While masculinity in Cicero’s world – and that of many of his later readers – is always a positive term, it’s also clear that its precise significance was just as contested then, albeit in different ways, and within different limits, as it is in the early 21st century. And just occasionally Cicero himself reveals the conscious effort involved in putting on a performance of authentic manliness.

The Neptunes’ Chad Hugo is pushing back against an effort by his estranged production partner, Pharrell Williams, to dismiss his copyright infringement lawsuit, accusing Williams of trying to erase his contributions to one of hip-hop’s most influential duos.

In a new court filing, Hugo and his lawyer, Brent Lehman, dispute Williams’ contention that the lawsuit identifies only one song at issue. Instead, Hugo says the case encompasses a much broader body of work stemming from compositions the two created during nearly 50 studio sessions between 2019 and 2021. He argues that Williams and his affiliated companies, record labels, and publishers control the records needed to identify how those compositions were ultimately released.
Hugo says he singled out EarthGang’s “U Gotta” as one example because he was allegedly removed from the track’s credits despite the recording artists themselves acknowledging his contributions.

“Defendants ask the court to write Chad Hugo out of The Neptunes on the pleadings, before a single document has been produced,” Hugo’s new filing, obtained by Rolling Stone, states. “But The Neptunes were two people. For three decades, Hugo and Pharrell Williams wrote and produced records together under that name. Hugo has always been at the center of The Neptunes success and is equally responsible for the duo’s special place in the industry. Over the past few years, Williams has sought to erase Hugo from one of the greatest hip-hip duos of all time. This case is about Williams’ effort to rewrite history and turn The Neptunes’ success into the work of only one person.”

Hugo calls Williams’ demand for more specific information “especially unfair,” arguing that he repeatedly sought royalty statements, financial records, and other documents between 2021 and 2024 but received “almost nothing, despite counsel’s acknowledgment that additional documents exist.”

Lawyers for Williams did not immediately respond to Rolling Stone’s request for comment on Friday. In his motion to dismiss, Williams argued that after three years and three versions of the complaint, Hugo failed to clearly identify a copyright claim that belongs in federal court.

He and his lawyers argued that Hugo first identified no specific songs in his original complaint, naming only the N.E.R.D. album No One Ever Really Dies. An amended complaint subsequently listed eight songs that were not on the album, but Hugo dropped all eight from his second amended complaint filed last month. The latest version of the complaint names only EarthGang’s “U Gotta,” without specifying whether Hugo is claiming rights to the musical composition, the sound recording or both, Williams argued.

“The [second amended complaint] is so vague and ambiguous with respect to the copyrights placed at issue that defendants cannot reasonably prepare a response,” Williams’ motion said. “As incomprehensible as it is, it appears that Hugo has no idea which compositions or sound recordings he supposedly authored — even though he claims to have been there, right by defendants’ side, the whole time.”

Williams argued that without a viable federal copyright claim, Hugo’s state-law claims involving breach of fiduciary duty and an incomplete accounting should also be dismissed, leaving him free to pursue those claims separately in state court.

In his lawsuit, Hugo said he and Williams co-founded the Neptunes and N.E.R.D., establishing themselves among the “most influential musical forces of their generation” with an innovative sound that helped shape modern hip-hop, R&B, and pop music. Hugo said his work as a songwriter, producer, arranger, and performer was central to their success, though Williams was the public face of their partnership.

“Although Defendant Williams often received greater public visibility, plaintiff’s contributions as a founding creative partner, co-writer, producer, and co-founder of both The Neptunes and N.E.R.D. were indispensable to the commercial value, goodwill, and brand recognition associated with these ventures,” Hugo’s second amended complaint read.

The complaint continued to identify No One Ever Really Dies as a source of alleged damages that could exceed $1 million. Hugo noted that the album debuted at Number 10 on the Billboard charts and has generated millions of streams.
Turns out that it’s tough to shoot in a whale’s stomach.

“Whalefall” director Brian Duffield is gleefully outlining some of the biggest hurdles while shooting his new movie. The premise for the film, in theaters now via 20th Century Studios, is simple: A young diver named Jay (Austin Abrams) is accidentally swallowed by a whale, ends up in its stomach and must escape before his tank of oxygen runs out. It’s a lean idea, but required an innovative and energetic leader like Duffield to get the claustrophobic shots done on practical sets.

“It’s such a small space and essentially a 360-degree set,” he says. “There’s a couple portals you can kind of shove a camera through, but it’s also somewhat full of water. All the lighting of the coil is inside the set. Basically everything that you would have on a normal movie set, we’re putting inside of a very small space. It’s also on a gimbal that’s rocking and rolling. So you take your normal film set footprint and then you put it into a bag. And then you also put Austin Abrams into the bag, and then sometimes other animals. If Austin’s wrong an inch, it doesn’t really work. Everyone’s cramped in this little doorway. But he can’t hear us, because the rubber is so thick inside.”
Duffield smiles at the outrageous setup.

“I was talking to a director,” he says. “He had a question and I sent him pictures of the set. And he was just like, ‘You’ve got to be joking.’ From when the whale is chewing Austin, it’s just a bunch of big, burly men jumping on the set and crushing down on him. And he’s in there, screaming and drowning with a real oxygen tank. I’m looking at this little monitor and if he needs help, it’s going to sound the exact same. Every time you call cut, you’re just hoping that the screaming stops. We had the studio come to set and watch this thing. From the outside it just looked so silly. I remember Disney safety reps would come and just be watching it, saying, ‘I genuinely don’t know if this is safe.’ But we worked hard, really hard to make sure Austin was safe.”

Everyone made it out of the shoot unharmed, but the finished product is filled with harrowing set-pieces that are sure to push audiences to the brink. Duffield understood the vision early on, as he reached out to novelist Daniel Kraus on social media when he first heard the premise of the novel of the same name, before it was even published. He read an advance copy of the 2023 book, and was quickly swept away with the cinematic promise it held. Duffield ended up co-writing the “Whalefall” script with Kraus.

“You get the initial ‘boy inside a whale’ story, which definitely tickled all the genre parts of my brain,” Duffield says. “The idea of making a movie that had never been made before is always really appealing to me. It’s instantly clear how challenging that was, and I was really looking for a challenge. I was hungry to just keep pushing myself and the crew that I had consistently been working with. I think we just had the appetite at the time to take a big swing.”

Duffield is no stranger to ambitious projects. He began his Hollywood career as a writer with a disparate group of scripts, including a big-budget sequel (2015’s “The Divergent Series: Insurgent”), a Western (2015’s “Jane Got a Gun”), a slasher (2017’s “The Babysitter”) and a sci-fi action movie (2020’s “Underwater”). He transitioned into an idiosyncratic directing career with 2020’s “Spontaneous” (logline: a romance is shaded by the fact that people start spontaneously combusting) and 2023’s “No One Will Save You,” a nearly dialogue-free alien invasion movie.

Beyond their high concepts, Duffield’s works are marked by an emotional heft, which is no different in “Whalefall.” Jay’s diving trip is prompted by him trying to locate the body of his estranged father Mitt (Josh Brolin) after he dies by suicide. He’d never be able make amends with, or come to an understanding with his father, a theme that resonates through much of the story.

“I don’t think I was looking for a father-son story, but I think I needed a father-son story,” Duffield, a parent himself, says. “As soon as I was reading it, I couldn’t stop thinking about … not the whale, but about Jay and Mitt in that relationship. I thought, ‘That was the magic trick of the book.’ You’re forgetting about squids and acid and you’re thinking more about how these two guys are thinking they want nothing more than to spend time together, but they can’t quite express how they need to spend time in a different way.”

While Abrams and Brolin were able to bring the emotional gravitas to flashback scenes chronicling key moments in their frayed relationship, shooting the in-whale scenes was the overarching creative challenge.

“I had plenty of directors come and visit and all of them just looked so baffled,” Duffield says. “I had general confusion about how we were doing what we were doing. The thing I’ve learned the most is the joy of making movies for me is the crew and getting to hire a lot of the same people over and over again. I think if I have any gift as a director, it’s hiring people that are extremely talented, Oscar winners and whatnot. I like spending time with them and feel comfortable asking advice. I trust them if I feel like they have a note or an idea — it’s probably good.”
It’s part of a larger ethos Duffield brings to every project.
“I want to feel the effort, and I want to feel like I’m becoming a better filmmaker because of it,” he says.

Benchmarks are the rulers of AI, in both senses of the word. As measuring sticks, they work according to an extremely simple logic: If you want to know what an AI model can do, devise a standardized test to gauge it. But AI benchmarks can also dominate the behavior of the entire field.

In 1987, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s first benchmark on automatic speech-to-text translation showed that state-of-the-art AI could not outperform so-called “dumb” statistical approaches. The poor performance helped to usher in an AI winter. For 25 years, interest in AI research waned and funding dried up.
Then, in 2012, another benchmark called ImageNet swung the pendulum back. An eight-layer neural network trounced other algorithms at classifying images and kicked off a “deep learning revolution.”

Nowadays, new AI benchmarks, geared at large language models such as OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, get created and solved with clockwork regularity, purporting to measure everything from domain-specific expertise to “general intelligence.” But rather than hail this trend as proof of AI’s skyrocketing potential, many in the field — skeptics and boosters alike — take it as evidence that benchmarking itself has become fatally flawed.

Moritz Hardt, a computer scientist and a director at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, agrees with this diagnosis. Shortly after the ImageNet result, he began to think that machine learning systems could game leaderboards “without doing anything intelligent.” “There’s no two ways about it,” he said. “The benchmarking ecosystem is broken.”

In his 2026 book The Emerging Science of Machine Learning Benchmarks, Hardt makes the provocative case that these measuring sticks have been broken for decades already: Benchmarks, he writes, are “the mistake that made machine learning.” Notably, he argues, instead of creating a replicability crisis, they drove legitimate progress anyway — “mostly by sheer luck,” in his view. By understanding why, we can explain how benchmarks have since lost this accidental credibility in the age of LLMs, and how they might regain it.
Quanta spoke to Hardt about what went wrong, and right, with benchmarks, and where to take them next. The interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.
Let’s get the basics straight: What even is a benchmark?

The recipe is simple. To evaluate a machine learning model, you take your data and split it into a training set and a test set. You let the model builders do whatever they want on the training set: Anything goes, no rules. But you use the test set only to compare and rank models — to have a leaderboard say, “This is currently state-of-the-art, this is number one, this is number two.”
So a benchmark for a large language model today, like GPT-6 Astra or Claude Fable, might test an ability to solve difficult math problems or find security bugs in software.

Right. The first benchmark, in fact, was created in 1959. It was a set of digits and letters printed on punch cards, meant to test how well different scanners could recognize written characters. Somebody introduced the train-test split and started a leaderboard.
It wasn’t like there was some master plan. But that’s what we now call benchmarking, and it’s been the engine of progress in AI for about 60 years or so.
What are benchmarks supposed to tell us?
Traditionally, a benchmark is supposed to be like a thermometer. People train a model to do something, and then you come up with some kind of measurement procedure to see how good the model is.
But in practice, benchmarking is more like a sports competition or a market. Benchmarks define the rules of the game, and people actively compete over them, and we let the best model win.

Any machine learning textbook will tell you about the “holdout method” — that you should lock away the test set, and only use it once to rank the models. If you ignore this, you’re on thin ice. You might get very misleading results because you’re evaluating models that in some sense have knowledge of the test set.

The fascinating thing is that machine learning as a discipline just ignored the warning. It took all these test sets and put them on the internet for everyone to use. It’s easy to put these test sets in a model’s development loop and to keep iterating on them.
Is that what’s “broken” about benchmarks?

If you look at a model’s accuracy numbers on one benchmark, and then you change the test set only slightly, you get completely different accuracy numbers. That’s the sense in which the benchmark is not working. If you have 90% accuracy on one dataset and 73% on another, which is it? I have no idea how good this model is.
OpenAI, Anthropic, and other technology companies still advertise benchmark numbers as a measurement of their models’ reasoning capabilities. Is that just nonsense?

These scores really get misused. If you say, “On this math benchmark, the model got a 90%, which means that the model is now equivalent to an expert mathematician,” you’re reading something into that number that gives you the wrong takeaway. We should avoid comparisons or conclusions that implicitly require the absolute number to make sense.
If the absolute numbers don’t make sense, how do you not end up with a replication crisis?

This is where things get really interesting. If, instead of absolute numbers, you look at rankings — relative comparisons between models — those rankings tend to be very stable across different datasets. And this has been pretty consistent across the history of machine learning. If one model gets 90% on a particular test set, and another model gets 80%, then the 90% model is the model you’d want to use in the real world. It’ll still do better on other datasets, even ones that are quite different than the test set.
That, to me, is the main reason why machine learning escaped a scientific crisis.
That’s surprising. So the 90% score doesn’t have much validity, but the fact that it “won” the competition does?
Yeah. So benchmarks tell you when you beat the previous best. And these improvement indicators are pretty reliable.

But it’s lucky that it worked as well as it did — we had no reason to expect this to be the case. And we don’t yet have a good comprehensive theory for why this happens. It’s mostly an empirical phenomenon.
But you also argue that now, in the era of large language models, benchmarks are no longer able to deliver this “accidental” reliability. Why not?

The stability of model rankings has one big caveat: Models need to train on the same training set. In the old days, this was always true. But we don’t know what LLMs were trained on. In fact, model builders can strategically assemble data mixes that best promote benchmark performance. It’s a little bit like studying to the test, which we all do in high school.

That’s why we’re currently in this benchmarking crisis — because it’s no longer true that the better model necessarily wins. A worse model might just put more effort into preparing for the specific benchmark.

This isn’t really a crime: It happens every time a new model is released. If you look at the notes on the latest version of Gemini or GPT, you’ll see that its performance on benchmarks that were released before the new model is often fantastic, while its performance on benchmarks released shortly after is way lower. That’s always an indication that the model was “post-trained” on the earlier benchmark — what some people call “benchmaxxed.” And it’s generally accepted.
Is there a way out of this benchmarking crisis, as you call it?

Let me tell you a story: At the 1968 Olympics in Mexico City, there was an American runner who was vastly favored to win the 1,500-meter race. He lost unexpectedly to a runner from the Kenyan highlands, by a wide margin. The Kenyan runner had trained at high elevation and was better prepared for competing at 7,500 feet above sea level. It caused some controversy: Should we outlaw altitude training? The consensus in the end was, just let everyone do it.

The problem is not so much that people optimize to the benchmarks — it’s that they optimize to different degrees. If everyone optimizes, or “altitude trains,” the absolute numbers will be inflated, but you can restore the validity of the rankings.
What would altitude training for AI benchmarks look like?
We don’t know ahead of time what went into these models, but we can train them for a little bit on benchmark-relevant data, just to make sure that we’re leveling the playing field somewhat.

In this new view of benchmarks, you would have no training set. You would have a test set, and you would also have some kind of protocol for preparing each of the models before you test them — that’s the altitude training.
But even if this works, we’re just back to where we started: progress indicators, but no valid measurements. Without that, how can we learn anything about how the models work?

This is a really interesting question. There’s something sad to the triumph of benchmarking, because it seems like we’re giving up what science is actually about: understanding the mechanisms. But if we had some kind of grand mathematical theory to build these models with, we wouldn’t need the benchmarks.
We don’t know how these models do it, and benchmarking won’t tell us.

But benchmarking can, in the long run, lead to new scientific knowledge. The CASP protein-folding benchmark advanced science without first insisting on a scientific theory of protein folding. That’s the paradoxical power of benchmarking in the sciences.
Astronomers discover a strange universal rule behind black hole eruptions
Scientists have uncovered a hidden rule that could explain and help predict when black holes unleash enormous jets into space.

- Scientists have discovered that black holes of vastly different sizes appear to launch powerful jets according to the same universal rule. The breakthrough could explain why some black holes suddenly erupt years after devouring a star and help astronomers predict when these spectacular outbursts will happen.

Astronomers have uncovered a surprising rule that appears to determine when black holes unleash powerful jets of material into space. Even though black holes can differ in mass by millions of times, researchers found that they seem to follow the same fundamental pattern when producing these enormous cosmic outflows.

The discovery, published in Nature Astronomy, suggests that black holes can activate their jets at the same critical stage of their feeding cycle, whether they weigh roughly 10 times as much as the Sun or millions of times more.

The research was led by Dr. Adelle Goodwin, an astrophysicist at Curtin University's International Centre of Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) and a Forrest Research Foundation Fellow, alongside co-author Dr. Andrew Mummery of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton.

The breakthrough emerged from years of studying unusual events in which supermassive black holes tear stars apart. By combining observations from telescopes in Australia, the United States, India, South Africa, and space, the scientists pieced together a clearer picture of how black holes behave as they consume matter.

Surprisingly, the crucial insight did not come while examining a telescope. It happened in a bar in Madrid, where Goodwin and Mummery were attending a scientific conference. During a conversation, they recognized that the same rule known to govern jet formation in relatively small black holes also seemed to apply to their supermassive counterparts.
Why Some Black Holes Erupt Years After Devouring Stars
One of the biggest mysteries the researchers wanted to explain was why black holes do not always launch jets at the same time.

When a supermassive black hole tears apart a star, it sometimes produces a powerful jet almost immediately. In other cases, the black hole appears relatively quiet for months or even years before suddenly producing a detectable radio outflow.
"We were looking at these events and asking why the timing was so different," said Dr. Goodwin.
"Then the pattern became clear. The delayed jets were appearing when the black hole's feeding rate dropped to the same critical point already known from much smaller black holes.
"That was the moment we realized this was not just a quirk of one type of black hole, but it looked like a rule that applied across the Universe."
Although black holes are often portrayed as cosmic vacuum cleaners that swallow anything nearby, their feeding behavior is far more complicated.

As material spirals toward a black hole, not all of it necessarily disappears beyond the event horizon, the boundary past which nothing can escape. Some matter can instead be expelled into space through powerful jets and other outflows.
"When a black hole tears apart a star, it does not swallow everything neatly," Dr. Goodwin said.
"Some of the material is consumed, and some is launched back into space in powerful jets and outflows.
"You can think of it as a black hole burp, except these burps can blast material across enormous distances and influence the galaxies around them."
These enormous outflows can carry energy and matter far from the black hole, potentially affecting the surrounding galaxy.
How Scientists Studied Supermassive Black Holes in Action
Astronomers have long suspected that black holes operate according to the same underlying physical laws regardless of their mass. Demonstrating that connection, however, has been difficult.
One major obstacle is time. The feeding behavior of a supermassive black hole can change over thousands of years, making it nearly impossible for astronomers to watch an entire cycle unfold.
Goodwin and her colleagues tackled this problem by examining rare events known as tidal disruption events.

These occur when a star passes too close to a supermassive black hole and experiences such extreme gravitational forces that it is torn apart. Some of the resulting debris falls toward the black hole, temporarily increasing its feeding activity.

Unlike the much longer changes normally associated with supermassive black holes, these dramatic episodes can play out over just a few years. That gives scientists an unusual opportunity to track how a giant black hole responds as its supply of material changes.

The team initially examined 20 tidal disruption events using observations collected in visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and radio wavelengths. They then selected 10 events for which the available data allowed them to reliably estimate both the rate at which the black hole was consuming matter and the timing of its radio outflows.
By comparing these events, the researchers identified a remarkably consistent pattern.
The observations revealed two distinct stages during which black holes can produce jets.
The first occurs early in the feeding process, when the black hole is consuming matter at an exceptionally high rate.
The second can happen much later, hundreds or even thousands of days after the star is initially destroyed.
During this delayed phase, jets appear when the black hole's feeding rate falls to approximately 2% of its Eddington limit.

The Eddington limit is a theoretical benchmark describing the point at which the outward pressure produced by radiation balances the inward pull of gravity. Astronomers use it to measure how intensely a black hole is feeding relative to a characteristic physical limit.
What makes the finding especially significant is that the same 2% threshold has already been linked to jet formation in much smaller black holes within our own Milky Way galaxy.
In other words, black holes separated by enormous differences in mass appear to activate delayed jets at essentially the same relative feeding rate.
"These black holes are separated by enormous differences in mass, but they appear to switch on their jets at the same point in the feeding process," Dr. Goodwin said.
"That tells us something fundamental about black holes: the physics does not seem to care how big they are."

The finding provides a potential explanation for an otherwise puzzling observation. Some black holes generate radio jets soon after destroying a star, while others appear inactive before producing powerful outflows much later.
Rather than behaving unpredictably, these delayed eruptions may be governed by a common physical threshold.
Predicting When Black Holes Will Launch Jets
Beyond revealing something fundamental about black hole physics, the discovery could help astronomers make much better use of powerful radio telescopes.

Observing time on major scientific facilities is limited and highly competitive. Researchers must carefully decide which objects to study, how frequently to observe them, and when they are most likely to reveal something important.
If astronomers can estimate when a black hole's feeding rate will approach the critical threshold, they may be able to predict when a delayed jet is likely to appear.

"Radio telescopes are incredibly powerful, but knowing when to look is just as important as knowing where to look," said Dr. Goodwin. "If we can anticipate when a black hole is more likely to launch a jet, we can run better targeted campaigns, waste fewer observations and improve our chances of catching these rare events at the moment they matter most."
This could reduce unnecessary follow-up observations while increasing the chances of detecting rare jet-launching episodes at crucial moments.

The implications are particularly important for Western Australia, which will host the low-frequency component of the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKA), one of the largest and most ambitious radio astronomy projects ever undertaken.

The Australian Government has invested $387 million in the SKA, while the project's total cost exceeds $2 billion. Making more efficient use of such an expensive facility could provide substantial benefits to astronomers and the wider scientific community, potentially allowing more important discoveries to be made with the available observing time.

As the next generation of astronomical surveys identifies growing numbers of tidal disruption events, researchers will face an increasingly difficult challenge in deciding which ones deserve closer attention.

The newly identified relationship between feeding rates and jet formation could provide a valuable guide, helping scientists focus their observations on the black holes most likely to produce detectable outflows.
A Black Hole Breakthrough Driven by Curiosity

Professor James Arvanitakis, Director of the Forrest Research Foundation, said the discovery highlights the importance of supporting early-career scientists who pursue ambitious questions without knowing in advance where the answers will lead.
This kind of open-ended investigation, often described as 'blue sky' research, can produce unexpected discoveries with benefits extending far beyond the original scientific question.
"The Forrest Research Foundation did not fund a predetermined answer, we backed an exceptional researcher with a difficult question," Professor Arvanitakis said.

"That question has led to a discovery of international significance. This is exactly why fundamental research matters - it expands what we know, sharpens how we use major scientific infrastructure and builds capability that reaches well beyond astronomy.
"The fact this discovery was driven from Western Australia speaks to the strength of our research ecosystem, and the value of giving outstanding people a reason to build their careers here."
By linking the behavior of relatively small black holes to that of supermassive giants, the findings strengthen the idea that the same basic physical processes operate across vastly different scales.
They also offer astronomers a more reliable way to anticipate one of the universe's most dramatic phenomena: the moment a black hole begins launching a powerful jet into space.

Oregon is turning to third-string quarterback Brock Thomas over Dylan Raiola with its College Football Playoff hopes on the line against Nebraska, according to CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz and Chris Hummer. It will be the first start of Thomas' career.

Thomas took the majority of first-team reps in practice throughout the week; he will get his first career start on Saturday. In his mid-week press conference, Ducks coach Dan Lanning explained the with Dante Moore still recovering from a concussion.

"[Saturday's performance] all plays into effect, and the body of work this week all plays into effect. The question was asked of me why not make the change sooner after the game; I think that's fair. On the same note, I think some of the positions we put [Raiola] in weren't successful opportunities as well," Lanning said. "I think we made some adjustments in getting the ball out a little quicker, creating some more open pictures that allowed Brock to do that.
"But you have to be able to protect the ball, that's a part of it, and like I said after the game, Dylan's also a guy that played really well against USC and you have to be aware of that too."

After throwing his second interception -- and completing just 31.6% of his passes -- Raiola was pulled in favor of Thomas against the Bruins. Thomas, a senior and a Eugene native, has been at Oregon since he joined the program as a walk-on in the 2023 recruiting cycle.

Despite his age, Thomas has very little game experience. His 15 pass attempts against UCLA make up almost half of his 36 career attempts. In that small sample size, Thomas has completed 72.2% of his throws for 302 yards and two touchdowns.

Coming out of high school, Thomas was the No. 96 quarterback and No. 10 player out of Oregon in the 2023 recruiting class, per 247Sports. He had scholarship offers from smaller programs like Air Force, Army, Eastern Washington and Portland State.

Instead of accepting one of those offers, Thomas chose to walk on at Oregon, and the Eugene native became a Duck. Thomas has stuck with the team ever since, despite being stuck well behind other quarterbacks like Bo Nix, Dillon Gabriel, Moore and Raiola.
Thomas didn't even attempt a pass until September of last year, when he went 0-for-1 in a 66-point win over Oklahoma State.

In last week's loss to UCLA, Thomas at least gave his team a chance to win, even if he didn't light the world on fire. The senior made smart decisions in the passing game, which was an upgrade over Raiola, although he did fumble the snap on a key fourth-and-1.

Now, in a surprising turn of events, the quarterback from Eugene will get the chance to lead Oregon to victory after waiting for an opportunity that was never guaranteed. Thomas has the makings of a folk hero if he can seize his opportunity on Saturday.
Coming out of Oregon's win over USC, Raiola was heralded as the example of a player who to reset a career that had been derailed at Nebraska.
Two weeks later, Raiola was watching from the bench as Thomas tried to steer Oregon to victory.

Against the Trojans, Raiola looked poised, confident and accurate. He completed 76% of his passes for 289 yards and two touchdowns. In fact, Raiola played so well that there were even faint questions about what Lanning would do if Moore returned from a concussion with Raiola igniting the offense.

Unfortunately for Lanning, that dilemma never presented itself. Moore remained out for the UCLA game, and Raiola looked like the player he was toward the end of his time at Nebraska. The junior was careless and inaccurate as he tried to do too much on several key plays.

As poorly as Raiola played against the Bruins, things took a downward turn for him in his second year at Nebraska. Entering college as a five-star recruit, Raiola approached his full potential in Lincoln and broke his fibula, which limited him to nine games last season.

With a rift brewing between Nebraska and Raiola's family, the two sides parted ways, and he landed at Oregon. The USC game looked like a big step in the right direction, but old habits emerged against UCLA. As a result, Raiola will have to wait for another opportunity down the line.
The Ducks entered the season as a national championship favorite, but they've become the nation's biggest disappointment.

There's still a tinge of hope for Oregon, but it will probably have to run the table, and this mess at quarterback won't make it any easier. Based on what we've seen out of the Ducks, they can't be trusted to go 7-0 against their remaining schedule.
There's at least a decent chance Oregon has three losses by Sunday. Nebraska is 5-1 and just took defending national champion Indiana to the wire, albeit in Lincoln.

Even if the Ducks go 6-1 with a loss to Ohio State, they'll need a lot of help to get into the playoff field. USC, Nebraska, Northwestern and Michigan would all need strong finishes to make those wins look as good as possible. Maybe that happens, but Oregon doesn't want to put itself at the mercy of the Big Ten's mushy middle.

Oregon probably needs Moore back at quarterback this season, which is not a sure thing, in order to have any shot at running the table. For now, though, the Ducks' fate is in the hands of Thomas and an offense that's searching for answers.

Leap seconds are a way to keep atomic-clock-driven UTC in line with astronomically kept Universal Time (UT1). Think of it like adding a little extra track for a train to keep running exactly parallel with another one. Rather than happening on a set interval—like a leap year—BIPM uses the average of hundreds of atomic clocks around the world and compares their time calculations to astronomical time to determine when a leap second is necessary. The most recent one was added in 2016.

Of course, adding track is no small effort, and it may seem like a lot of hassle for a measly second. But UTC is vital for all sorts of technology given the number of APIs and databases that rely on it. Introducing a leap second helped keep UTC and UT1 aligned, but it also wrought havoc on various systems running on UTC and forced companies to figure out how to deal with them when they were added every few years.

A number of tech companies like Google and Meta use “a ‘smear’ method of dealing with leap seconds,” Judah Levine, a fellow at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, writes in an email. In essence, they spread a leap second out over the course of a day or so in tiny increments. But leap seconds have thrown off other systems; the airline Qantas, for example, saw its booking system borked by a leap second in 2012.

Adding a leap second is hard enough as it is. But the odds of having to add a negative leap second have been rising in part because Earth has picked up rotational speed in recent years due to climate change. (There’s always a climate angle.) Melting ice has caused a shift in the planet’s gravity so extreme that a negative leap second may have been required as soon as 2029, according to a 2024 Nature study. Part of the calculus of ditching the leap second altogether was that going negative isn’t worth the risk.

“There are continuing problems with positive leap seconds even after 50 years, and the concern was that the negative leap second would be much more serious because its effects had never been tested,” Levine says.

BIPM time department director Patrizia Tavella confirmed those concerns in an email to WIRED. “The probability of a negative leap second convinced us [to] set the application date in 2027,” she wrote, adding that there was added urgency following tests by an industry standards group that “showed several failures with a negative leap.”

Tavella says the group is waiting until May 20 2027 to implement it because it's the anniversary of 1875 signing of the Metre Convention, creating BIPM, as well as Metrology Day. In other words, it’s the perfect time to mark the passing of time—or more accurately, the lack thereof.

The death of the leap second makes life easier for everyone now. “The nice fact is that we have nothing to do!” Tavella says. “Just continue to accumulate second[s] and ‘normal’ minutes of 60 seconds.”
Levine concurs, writing that “life will have one less hassle.”

But kicking the can on adding leap seconds doesn’t mean atomic time and astronomical time won’t continue to drift apart. That’s why BIPM also agreed to create a leap hour. Given how long it takes leap seconds to add up, a leap hour is millennia away. (There are, after all, 3,600 seconds in an hour.)

“We do not speak of leap hour yet,” Tavella says. “If systems rely on UTC, they have nothing to do. If they rely on UT1, they have to be able to use the information UT1-UTC which, in [the] future, will be larger than 1 second.”
In other words, not our problem, and good luck to future generations!

When the European thermal-imagery company constellr began working with Space Inventor on its next generation of satellites, some of the most important details of the spacecraft had yet to be finalized.

The Munich-based firm knew it wanted its HiVE, or High-precision Versatile Ecosphere, constellation to measure temperatures from space with the precision needed for agricultural applications and urban planning. But the requirements for the payload’s size, weight and power were still evolving.

That presented what can be a familiar tradeoff in the small satellite community. Work on satellite buses often begins before every detail of a payload has been finalized. If engineers lock in the spacecraft design too early, the payload may need to conform to the bus. If the payload needs new iterations, the bus may require an extensive – and expensive – redesign.

But Space Inventor, the Danish manufacturer, took a different approach. Instead of demanding the payload fit a standardized satellite bus, it adapted its BIG CAT 600 bus as constellr’s requirements evolved.

“We needed a platform built around the payload, not the other way around,” said Marius Bierdel, constellr’s co-founder and vice president of program management. “Space Inventor’s system-level approach means our thermal sensors perform exactly as designed once they’re in orbit.”

That ability to repeatedly modify the spacecraft is the centerpiece of Space Inventor’s pitch to operators who need to build payload-centric mini-constellations. Unlike megaconstellations numbering in the hundreds or thousands, mini-constellations typically range from a few satellites to a few dozen and can target specific geographies or niche capabilities.

“These are high state-of-the-art payloads that often are still in development when we start building the bus,” said Jan Smolders, the chief commercial officer at Space Inventor. As one batch is being built, he said, Space Inventor is already applying lessons learned to the design of the next.
“The standardization is in the satellite modules, not in the bus,” he added.
Mini-constellations occupy a middle ground in the satellite market.

Their smaller scale offers flexibility. Operators may want to incorporate lessons from the first satellites into later iterations. Or, as technology advances, they may want to upgrade the instruments.
Space Inventor designed its BIG CAT family of services for exactly those moments.

The BIG CAT 100, 300 and 600 platforms are sized for different spacecraft classes, but each is configurable rather than fixed. That means if a mission suddenly needs more power, improved pointing performance or a new communications capability, Space Inventor can often accommodate these changes by swapping out bus modules, rather than redesigning a spacecraft from scratch.

That philosophy of iteration is especially helpful in rapidly changing fields such as thermal imaging, space domain awareness and in-orbit servicing. It also means Space Inventor can avoid locking in a design around requirements developed years before launch.
Space Inventor pairs its modular approach with another strategy: making most of its components itself.

The company manufactures nearly all of its components – with the exception of propulsion – in house at its factory in Aalborg, Denmark, offering more control over its design and less exposure to the volatility of the supply chain.

If a new requirement calls for a modified PCB, Space Inventor can update the design, machine a revised housing, assemble the new component and test the change, all under the same roof. Such a change ordered from an outside supplier might take about six weeks. Space Inventor can make the same change in roughly one week, Smolders said.
“Because we make everything in house, we can easily add new modules to facilitate changing requirements, very fast,” he said.
This gives Space Inventor tighter quality control and reduces exposure to supply chain shortages.

Space Inventor also maintains a stock of its components, allowing it to offer next-day shipping. That reduces the risk that a small component or a supplier delay holds up the production of a spacecraft.
For mini-constellation operators, this model makes it easier to change later satellites based on what they’ve learned from earlier ones.
The same configurable approach that Space Inventor uses for commercial missions also underpins its offerings for the defense community.
Rather than only offering military customers a satellite bus, the company can pair a BIG CAT platform with a mission-specific payload to provide a turnkey system.
Space Inventor’s defense-specific Apex Predator series includes BC Lynx and BC Leopard, two turnkey surveillance solutions built on its BIG CAT platform.

Lynx is designed to detect radio-frequency emissions, geolocate their source and identify activity that may warrant further investigation. Leopard can then be tasked with capturing high-resolution optical or thermal imagery in the same area.
The approach follows a “tip-and-cue” model, with one sensor identifying a potential target and then directing another sensor to collect more detailed information.

The company has also developed a business case for detecting and investigating maritime activity in the heavily trafficked Baltic Sea, bordered by NATO members and Russia. There, Lynx satellites can identify anomalous RF emissions that could reveal dark vessels or help locate sources of GPS spoofing. It can then cue a Leopard satellite to collect additional intelligence.
This space-based approach to surveillance, Smolders argues, offers a cost-effective complement to expensive drones and stealth aircraft that can only monitor a relatively contained area at once.

“For the cost of one or two F-35s, you can actually get the intelligence to tell those planes where to go,” he said. “Affordable, proven ISR capability is ready to deploy in Europe today, with Space Inventor at the forefront of turning that capability into operational missions, but the decision-makers need to know about it.”
U.S. Special Operations forces will adopt a new face and breathing protection system after the Pentagon and Avon Protection announced a contract on Oct. 9.

The MITR half-mask and goggle system is designed to protect wearers from dangerous chemicals and toxic substances in the atmosphere, including lead powder from gunfire, ballistics and poisonous substances like fentanyl.

Casey Galligan, Avon’s senior director for the U.S. Homeland Security and the Department of Defense, told Defense News that fentanyl and chemicals found in drug labs are now part of a wide array of hazards that special warfare operators must guard against, in addition to biological weapons and other breathing hazards.

“Precursor drug chemicals now are a huge issue that are just as dangerous as a chemical hazard,” Galligan said. “As an operator, every day you’re doing something quasi-dangerous, particularly those at the frontline doing maneuver. This is not meant to replace a full-face respirator. A split system gives you options.”

The half-mask system walks the line between an N-95 disposable mask and a heavy, full-face respirator. The goggles and half-mask can be worn linked together or separated, giving operators a lightweight option that will give them eye and breathing protection as needed without requiring them to carry heavy full-face respirator masks.

The MITR features positive pressure-sealed goggles to stop hazardous chemicals from getting in around its edges. The system features sweat drainage outlets inside the goggles and blows cool air into them from both sides, preventing lens fogging.
A former U.S. Army Green Beret, Galligan said the system provides safety against toxic materials while allowing wearers to breathe easier — literally.

“If you don’t always want to be wearing a full-face respirator, and you’re worried about different levels of threats, this is a half-pound and easy to put on. You can wear it with a head harness or with helmet attachments,” he explained.
Half-mask systems are not new, but the MITR system has evolved constantly to incorporate new evolutions in technology to reach its current capabilities.
“We’ve been going through iterations and continuing to improve it,” said Galligan, adding that the U.S. is joining Canada and another FVEY nation in purchasing the system.
Elite warfare units of U.S. Special Operations are already wearing the new half-mask and goggles in the field, he disclosed.
“We’ve fielded it to units already. Some are en route right now, being delivered,” Galligan said. “The feedback I get talking with end users is pretty amazing.”

The Defense Department’s decision to equip SOCOM operators with improved breathing equipment follows a November 2025 report, called the SOF Cancer Study, which revealed that SOF operators face an 18% higher risk of cancer than non-SOF personnel due to hazardous materials in their environments that they are exposed to constantly in the line of duty.
Shifting to a half-mask system could mark the dawn of a new era in how military service members approach facial protection overall.
“When you see the tip of the spear using it, it’s going to make it a lot more acceptable,” Galligan said.
